conventional_description: In Western medicine, allergic colitis refers to inflammation of the colon triggered by an allergic response, most commonly to food proteins. It is frequently seen in infants as food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis, causing diarrhea, blood-streaked stools, and abdominal discomfort. In adults, it can arise from food sensitivities and may present with similar symptoms, including mucus in the stool and cramping. Diagnosis usually involves stool tests, colonoscopy with biopsy, and elimination diets to identify trigger foods.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management focuses on identifying and eliminating the offending food allergen. For infants, this often means switching to a hypoallergenic formula or the mother avoiding dairy and soy while breastfeeding. In persistent cases, medications such as corticosteroids or aminosalicylates may be used to reduce inflammation. Probiotics and supportive care for hydration are also common.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the Spleen is the central organ of digestion, responsible for transforming food into Qi and transporting fluids. When the Spleen is weak - due to poor diet, overwork, or constitutional factors - it fails to manage fluids, leading to the accumulation of Dampness. This Dampness is heavy and sticky, and it can sink into the Large Intestine, causing the loose, mucus-filled stools characteristic of allergic colitis. A pale, puffy tongue with teeth marks is a classic sign of this Spleen weakness.
The Liver governs the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body. Emotional stress, frustration, or anxiety can cause Liver Qi to stagnate. In TCM, the Liver has a tendency to 'invade' the Spleen when it's stuck, like a stressed boss taking it out on a subordinate. This disrupts the Spleen's digestive function, leading to sudden cramping and urgent diarrhea that often strikes at moments of stress. The pattern is so common that it has its own classic formula.
When Dampness lingers, it can combine with Heat - often from a diet rich in greasy, spicy foods or from a hot, humid climate - to create Damp-Heat. This pathogen is like a toxic steam that inflames the intestinal lining, producing the hallmark symptoms of an acute flare: urgent, burning diarrhea with blood and mucus, a feeling of incomplete evacuation, and a red tongue with a thick yellow coating. This is an excess pattern that needs to be cleared quickly.
In chronic, long-standing cases, the digestive fire of the Kidneys may also become depleted. The Kidneys provide the foundational Yang energy that warms the Spleen and intestines. When this fire is low, the body can't properly cook food, leading to chronic diarrhea with undigested food, cold limbs, and a sore back. This deep deficiency pattern often underlies lifelong gut sensitivity and requires long-term rebuilding.
Because allergic colitis can stem from weakness, stagnation, heat, or cold - and often a mix - TCM doesn't offer a one-size-fits-all solution. Instead, a practitioner reads the specific signs: the stool quality, the tongue, the pulse, the triggers, and the accompanying symptoms to identify which pattern is dominant. This allows treatment to be precisely targeted, not just at the inflamed colon but at the whole system that created it.

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by listening closely to the story of the bowel movements. The quality of the stool - whether it is watery, sticky, contains mucus or blood, or includes undigested food - is a primary clue. The timing of symptoms, what makes them better or worse, and the presence of pain, bloating, or urgency all guide the diagnosis toward one pattern or another.
When the stool is urgent, burning, and mixed with mucus and bright blood, and the person feels an unproductive urge to go again right after a bowel movement, Damp-Heat in the Large Intestine is the likely picture. The tongue will appear red with a thick, yellow, greasy coating, and the pulse will feel rapid and slippery. This is an acute, inflammatory state that needs clearing.
If instead the main story is chronic loose stools, fatigue, poor appetite, and a heavy, bloated sensation after eating, the root lies in a Spleen deficiency. When these symptoms come with a pale, puffy tongue with teeth marks and a weak pulse, it points to Spleen Qi Deficiency.
If dampness is more prominent - with a greasy white tongue coating, heavy limbs, and a feeling of muddled thinking - then Spleen Deficiency with Dampness is the deeper diagnosis. In very long-standing cases, cold signs like chilly limbs, lower back soreness, and early-morning diarrhea indicate that the deficiency has deepened into Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency.
Another distinct story emerges when diarrhea and cramping flare up exactly with emotional stress, and the pain eases after a bowel movement. This is Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Spleen; the tongue may be normal or slightly red on the edges, and the pulse feels wiry.
Finally, if the pain is fixed and stabbing, with dark blood clots in the stool and a dark tongue showing stasis spots, the picture has evolved into Blood Stagnation with Heat, a more complicated chronic presentation.

patterns.symptoms: ["Diarrhea with mucus or blood and foul smell", "Urgent, painful straining and incomplete evacuation", "Burning sensation at the anus", "Scanty, dark yellow urine", "Feeling of body heat, thirst, and heavy limbs", "Poor appetite with nausea and abdominal fullness"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or spicy foods, Spicy food and alcohol, Emotional stress, anger, or frustration, Hot, humid weather, Irregular eating habits or overeating
patterns.better_with: Light, bland, well-cooked meals, Adequate hydration with warm fluids, Rest and reduced activity, Cool, dry environment
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body accumulates excessive Dampness and Heat - often from a diet rich in greasy, spicy, or sweet foods, or from hot, humid environments - these pathogenic factors sink downward and lodge in the Large Intestine. The Heat irritates and inflames the intestinal lining, while the heavy, sticky Dampness blocks the normal flow of Qi. This combination produces the hallmark symptoms of urgent, burning diarrhea with mucus and blood, and a persistent sensation of incomplete evacuation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a thick, yellow, greasy coating, thickest at the centre and root. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and rapid (数 shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, spicy, and sweet foods, along with alcohol, directly generate Dampness and Heat in the body, which then pour down into the intestines. Emotional stress can cause Qi stagnation that transforms into Heat, adding fuel to the fire. A bland, well-cooked diet and warm fluids are easy for the weakened Spleen to process, helping it recover its function of transforming and transporting fluids, thereby clearing Dampness. Rest conserves Qi for healing, and a cool, dry environment does not add external Damp-Heat to the internal condition.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid all greasy, fried, spicy, and heavily sweetened foods, as well as alcohol and raw, cold dishes, which directly add Dampness and Heat. Base meals around well-cooked, bland, and easily digested foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and lean protein. Drink warm water or barley tea throughout the day to help flush Dampness. Rest is essential during acute flare-ups; gentle movement like walking can support Qi flow once the worst has passed.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is responsible for transforming food and fluids into usable Qi and for keeping Dampness in check. When Spleen Qi is weak, it fails to transport and transform fluids, allowing Dampness to accumulate. This internal Dampness then pours down into the Large Intestine, making the stools loose, unformed, and sometimes mixed with mucus. The result is the chronic, bloating diarrhea typical of allergic colitis.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, white greasy coating, moist surface. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slowed-down (Huan), soft and lacking force, especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen Deficiency with Dampness means the Spleen's ability to transform and transport fluids is weak. Cold and raw foods further damage Spleen Yang and add Dampness, worsening loose stools and bloating. Overeating overwhelms the Spleen. Warm, cooked foods and rest support Spleen Qi, helping it to dry up Dampness and form normal stool. Damp weather adds external dampness, while gentle movement helps Qi circulate to resolve internal dampness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like congee, steamed vegetables, and soups. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that create more Dampness. Add a little ginger or cardamom to meals to warm the digestion. Gentle walking after meals helps Qi move without overstraining the Spleen. Keep the abdomen warm with a belly band or warm compress.

Warm, cooked foods are easier for the weakened Spleen to digest, while cold and raw foods add dampness and further burden digestion.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat smaller, regular meals to avoid overloading the Spleen. Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that create dampness. Incorporate gentle exercise like walking or yoga to keep Qi moving smoothly. Practice stress management techniques such as deep breathing or meditation, as emotional tension directly triggers this pattern.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen and Kidneys are the body’s digestive fire. When their Yang is deficient, the body can’t warm the intestines or fully break down food. This leads to chronic loose stools, undigested food, and a deep internal coldness that shows up as cold limbs and a sore back. In allergic colitis, this yang weakness makes the bowel lining fragile and hypersensitive, triggering diarrhea especially in the early morning when the body’s fire is at its lowest.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen, puffy body with teeth marks and a white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, weak, and slow, especially feeble in both Chi (third) positions and the right Guan (middle) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: In Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency, the body’s internal fire is low. Cold foods and environments further drain this fire, worsening diarrhea. Warmth, rest, and moxibustion add yang energy, helping the Spleen and Kidney to transform and transport food properly, firming stools and relieving cold pain. Early morning is when yang qi is weakest, so symptoms like dawn diarrhea appear; keeping warm at that time is especially helpful.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat only warm, well-cooked foods; avoid all cold drinks, raw vegetables, and dairy. Keep the abdomen and lower back warm, especially in the early morning. Gentle moxibustion on the belly button area daily can help restore yang. Adequate rest is essential-overwork depletes yang further.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When Damp-Heat lingers in the intestines over a long period, it can scorch the delicate blood vessels of the gut lining. This heat thickens the blood and slows its flow, creating stasis - a kind of painful, stuck congestion. The result is a fixed, stabbing abdominal pain and stools that contain dark, clotted blood, especially at night when the body’s circulation naturally slows.
Think of it like a slow-burning fire that dries up a riverbed, leaving behind thick, dark sludge. The heat also agitates the mind, leading to irritability and a thirsty feeling where you want to wet your mouth but not actually drink much.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: reddish-purple body with purple stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, and a thin dry yellow coating. Pulse: choppy (涩, sè) and rapid (数, shuò), often wiry at the left Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy and greasy foods add heat to the body, worsening blood stasis and inflammation. Emotional stress stirs up Liver Qi, which can invade the intestines and exacerbate stasis. Rest and cooling foods help clear heat and calm the blood, while gentle movement prevents stagnation without overexertion.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat cooling, blood-nourishing foods like spinach, celery, cucumber, and a little lean protein. Avoid spicy, greasy, deep-fried foods, and alcohol, which add heat and thicken the blood. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps Qi and blood flow without exhausting you. Manage stress with meditation or deep breathing, as frustration stirs up Liver Qi and worsens stasis.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with allergic colitis?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture can help regulate the digestive system by calming inflammation, reducing pain, and restoring the smooth flow of Qi. Points on the abdomen and legs are commonly used to strengthen the Spleen and clear Dampness. Many patients find that regular sessions reduce the frequency and severity of flare-ups.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results with TCM?
faqs.answer: Acute symptoms like diarrhea and cramping often improve within the first 2-3 weeks of herbal treatment. However, deeper healing of the gut and a reduction in food sensitivities typically takes 2-3 months of consistent care. Chronic cases that have been present for years may require 6 months or longer to fully resolve.

faqs.question: Can I combine TCM herbs with my current medications?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes, but you must inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor. Some herbs can interact with immunosuppressants or corticosteroids, so professional guidance is essential. Never stop prescribed medications abruptly. Always bring a full list of your medications to your TCM consultation.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid while undergoing TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: In general, avoid raw, cold, greasy, and spicy foods, as well as dairy products, which tend to generate Dampness and burden the Spleen. Favour warm, cooked, easily digestible foods like congee, soups, and steamed vegetables. Your practitioner may give you more specific advice based on your pattern.

faqs.question: Does stress really cause my flare-ups? And can TCM help?
faqs.answer: Yes, stress is a major trigger for many people because it directly disrupts the Liver's ability to regulate digestion. TCM has specific herbal formulas and acupuncture protocols to smooth Liver Qi and protect the Spleen from this stress impact. Many patients find that as their stress response improves, their gut becomes much less reactive.

faqs.question: Will my symptoms come back after I stop treatment?
faqs.answer: The goal of TCM is to correct the underlying imbalance, not just suppress symptoms. When treatment is successful, the gut becomes stronger and less reactive, so symptoms are less likely to return. However, maintaining a healthy diet and managing stress are important for long-term results. Some patients benefit from occasional 'maintenance' treatments.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for children with allergic colitis?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be very safe and effective for children when administered by a qualified practitioner. Herbal doses are adjusted for the child's weight, and acupuncture may be replaced with acupressure or gentle pediatric massage (tuina). Always work with a practitioner experienced in pediatric care.

faqs.question: How does TCM diagnose my specific pattern?
faqs.answer: A TCM practitioner will take a detailed history, focusing on your bowel movements, pain, triggers, diet, and emotional state. They will also examine your tongue and feel your pulse. These signs together reveal which organ systems are involved and whether the condition is more excess or deficiency. This allows for a tailored treatment plan.

research.title: Acupuncture combined with Chinese herbal medicine for ulcerative colitis: a clinical study
research.description: This study evaluated the efficacy of acupuncture combined with oral Chinese herbal medicine in patients with ulcerative colitis. Results showed significant improvement in clinical symptoms, endoscopic scores, and inflammatory markers compared to baseline, suggesting that integrated TCM therapy can effectively induce remission and reduce mucosal inflammation.
research.periodical: Authors not specified. Acupuncture combined with Chinese herbal medicine for ulcerative colitis: a clinical study. Shanghai Journal of Acupuncture and Moxibustion, 2021.

research.title: Tong Xie Yao Fang: A Classic Chinese Medicine Prescription with Potential for the Treatment of Ulcerative Colitis
research.description: A review of pharmacological and clinical evidence for Tong Xie Yao Fang, a classic formula for Liver-Spleen disharmony, in treating ulcerative colitis. The review highlights its anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and gut-barrier protective effects, supporting its use for stress-aggravated colitis.
research.periodical: Li J, et al. Tong Xie Yao Fang: A Classic Chinese Medicine Prescription with Potential for the Treatment of Ulcerative Colitis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine, 2021; 2021: 5578639.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for ulcerative colitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials assessing Chinese herbal medicine as an adjunct to conventional therapy for ulcerative colitis. The analysis found that herbal medicine significantly improved clinical remission rates and reduced relapse, with a favorable safety profile, though most trials were of moderate quality.
research.periodical: Zhang C, et al. Chinese herbal medicine for ulcerative colitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, 2018; 33(Suppl 3): 256-257.
